themes.theme: Foreign Aid Cuts, Global Health & Federal Policy
themes.briefing:
The dismantling of USAID under the current federal policy environment is generating measurable and potentially catastrophic public health consequences globally. Contrary to assertions amplified by Elon Musk — who reposted and endorsed a claim that no child died as a result of USAID cuts — available evidence points to a significant and accelerating mortality toll[29]. USAID is estimated to have saved approximately 92 million lives over the past two decades, including 30.4 million children under five, establishing it as one of the most consequential instruments of American soft power and global health stabilization[29].

The withdrawal of that funding is now producing a measurable reversal in decades of progress. Roughly 200,000 more children are believed to have died in 2025 compared to 2024, marking the first time in thirty years that positive global health trends have moved in the wrong direction[29]. Over 1,300 health and family planning clinics have shuttered worldwide as a direct consequence of the cuts, and Lancet modeling projects the policy trajectory could result in 14 million deaths by 2030[29]. The exposure is particularly acute in fragile states: in the Democratic Republic of Congo, 89 percent of the AIDS response was previously funded by the United States, leaving virtually no institutional redundancy to absorb the loss[29]. The strategic and humanitarian calculus here is unambiguous — federal decisions made in Washington are translating into excess mortality at a scale that will compound over the remainder of the decade.

references.title: Yes, the Cuts to USAID Have Killed

themes.theme: Iran War, Middle East Escalation & U.S. Foreign Policy
themes.briefing:
The U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding, signed less than two weeks ago, is rapidly unraveling. Iran has attacked commercial vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz on multiple occasions, prompting renewed American military strikes and subsequent Iranian retaliation against U.S. military assets[1,3]. Professor Robert Pape, whose prior-week predictions on commercial shipping attacks, Strait of Hormuz pressure intensification, and Israeli military stiffening in Lebanon have all materialized, assesses that the MOU's collapse was foreseeable and that worse outcomes remain ahead[3]. Commercial traffic through the Strait remains far below prewar levels, and IRGC-linked Iranian media has renewed internal debate over whether Iran should move openly toward acquiring nuclear weapons[2,3]. The strategic architecture underpinning the ceasefire framework is therefore deteriorating on multiple fronts simultaneously.

The diplomatic picture is compounded by sharply conflicting interpretations of what the MOU actually obligates Iran to do. The U.S. and Iran hold incompatible readings of its terms regarding safe passage of commercial vessels, and one credible analytical framing characterizes the current arrangement not as a negotiated settlement but as an unacknowledged American capitulation — with the Strait quasi-open but effectively operating at Iranian sufferance[1]. Iran's nuclear program remains substantively unresolved, and the ambiguity surrounding its 60 percent-enriched uranium stockpile — which experts assess could be weaponized — has not been dispelled by administration claims to the contrary[5]. Israel continues pressing for broader regional military action, adding a further destabilizing variable to an already fragile equilibrium[3].

The strategic and economic costs of this trajectory extend beyond the immediate theater. The Iran war has accelerated the development of alternative payment systems that bypass dollar-denominated transactions, with China actively facilitating workarounds to the dollar-centered global payments infrastructure[4]. While the dollar still dominates foreign exchange — involved in roughly 89 percent of transactions despite the U.S. accounting for only about 10 percent of world exports — the war's handling has eroded American credibility as both a reliable ally and a credible adversary, weakening the non-military coercive leverage that dollar primacy historically provided[4]. Within the administration, the departure of Joe Kent, former Director of the National Counterterrorism Center, who resigned in March over the Iran war, signals ongoing internal divisions over strategy that continue to shape policy debates[2]. Taken together, the operational, diplomatic, and systemic indicators point toward a sustained period of elevated risk with no clear off-ramp.

themes.briefing:
The first half of 2026 has exposed a significant and potentially destabilizing paradox at the heart of the AI investment cycle: the hyperscalers driving the buildout are themselves underperforming the market they are reshaping. Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle have collectively lagged broader indices, with Microsoft down 20% and Oracle down 30% in June alone, even as these firms commit a staggering $805 billion in capital expenditure for the year — consuming 93% of their operating cash flows, up from just 33% in 2023[21]. The infrastructure spend is now feeding back into macroeconomic conditions in measurable ways, with the AI buildout contributing to elevated electronics and electricity costs that are pushing inflation to a three-year high, PCE at 4.1% and core PCE at 3.4%[21]. Meanwhile, AI quarterly revenues are now exceeding quarterly capex depreciation expense, though cumulative historic depreciation has not yet been recovered — a signal that the sector is approaching, but has not yet crossed, the threshold of genuine financial justification[24].

The market's structural response to this pressure is a rotation away from the Magnificent Seven toward new sectoral leaders, with memory chip manufacturers emerging as unexpected beneficiaries. Samsung, Micron, and SK Hynix have entered the ranks of the world's most valuable public companies, surpassing Berkshire Hathaway and JP Morgan Chase[21] — a trend underscored by SK Hynix's market capitalization overtaking Samsung Electronics' for the first time[24]. At the same time, broader market directionality is deteriorating. With consumer spending growing at only 0.5% in Q1 — its weakest pace in four years — and markets pricing a 64% probability that incoming Fed Chair Kevin Warsh raises rates as early as September[21], the macro backdrop is increasingly hostile. Analysts warn that this combination of slowing consumption, rising inflation, and rate uncertainty creates conditions consistent with a nervous market top at the midyear mark[22].

On the geopolitical dimension, the AI investment race carries compounding national security implications that Washington has yet to resolve coherently. Chinese AI labs, including Zhipu AI and DeepSeek, are releasing open-weight models that can be downloaded, modified, and operated without external oversight — and Zhipu AI's GLM-5.2 can already match Anthropic's restricted Mythos model on certain cybersecurity tasks, including the identification of software vulnerabilities[23]. Notably, Chinese labs are achieving this with talent averaging just 1.6 years of experience per hire, compared to 5.5 years for equivalent U.S. roles, suggesting a deliberate strategy of deploying volume over seniority[24]. Anthropic's temporary suspension of its most capable models following U.S. government restrictions illustrated the fragility of the current access regime; critics including former export control official Saif Khan argue that restricting American AI availability while Chinese alternatives remain consistently accessible risks degrading U.S. cyber defenses rather than protecting them[23]. Separately, proposed S&P and Nasdaq rule changes that would accommodate mega-cap IPOs — widely understood to benefit companies like SpaceX — could further concentrate market risk and undermine the diversification assumptions that passive investors have relied upon[20], adding yet another structural vulnerability to an already unsettled investment landscape.

themes.briefing:
The most acute domestic flashpoint on immigration this cycle involves the targeted deportation of Haitian residents from Springfield, Ohio — a case that has escalated to the Supreme Court with deeply consequential implications. Timothy Snyder argues that the Court's majority ruling was 'openly counter-factual,' disregarding a lower district court's February finding that the deportation decision was racially motivated[28]. The political origins of the Springfield campaign — traced to coordinated rhetoric from JD Vance, Donald Trump, and far-right actors alleging Haitians were 'eating pets,' 'probably have AIDS,' and 'poisoning the blood' of America — make this more than an immigration enforcement dispute; Snyder frames it explicitly as ethnic cleansing, enabled by juridical rationalization[28]. The over 10,000 Haitians targeted had been residing lawfully under Temporary Protected Status, granted in the wake of a catastrophic earthquake and subsequently extended following the assassination of Haiti's president[28]. The Court's willingness to sidestep the racial evidence sets a precedent with broad implications for how identity-based targeting can be insulated from legal challenge.

A parallel but distinct identity-and-rights struggle is unfolding in the American West, where the Navajo Nation, Hopi Tribe, and San Juan Southern Paiute Tribe have secured a landmark water rights settlement — the largest in U.S. tribal history — only to see it obstructed by four Upper Basin states[27]. Colorado, New Mexico, Utah, and Wyoming have formally opposed the Northeastern Arizona Indian Water Rights Settlement Act, citing state water interests, and specifically objecting to a provision permitting tribes to lease water to fast-growing Phoenix-area municipalities[27]. The human stakes are unambiguous: a third of homes on Hopi and Navajo reservations currently lack running water, with elderly residents hauling untreated water from livestock windmills[27]. The $5 billion federal infrastructure package tied to the settlement represents a concrete test of whether tribal sovereignty and historical rights can be operationalized against entrenched regional water politics — or whether legal recognition continues to outpace material delivery.

The theoretical underpinnings of immigration and national identity are also under renewed scrutiny. A Slow Boring analysis drawing on a Dutch PvdA minister's argument highlights a structural asymmetry: the United States benefits from an explicit 'propositional nationalism' — civic identity rooted in ideals rather than ethnicity — that gives American social democrats a rhetorical and political tool unavailable to their European counterparts[25]. The piece illustrates this through New York City's own Dutch heritage, noting that the city's traditions of tolerance predate the republic itself, embedded in the founding culture of New Amsterdam and still visible in civic symbols like the orange and blue of the Mets and Knicks[25]. This historical lens is analytically useful: it suggests that American pluralism is not a fragile modern experiment but a deeply rooted institutional inheritance — one that the Springfield case puts under direct stress.

themes.theme: U.S. Elections, Party Politics & Democratic Landscape
themes.briefing:
The Democratic Party's internal fault lines are on full display heading into the 2026 midterm cycle, with New York's June primaries offering a Rorschach test for competing strategic visions. Three candidates backed by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani defeated establishment incumbents, most notably Brad Lander's 32-point rout of Rep. Dan Goldman, fueling comparisons to a Tea Party-style insurgency on the left[14,17]. Yet the picture is more ambiguous than either side claims: moderate Democrat Cait Conley simultaneously won the competitive NY-17 primary by 18 points, suggesting the intraparty contest ended closer to a draw than a progressive wave[14]. Analysts parsing the implications for party brand must grapple with a key measurement problem — national DSA favorability sits at just 5%, but that figure is selectively alarming given that only 12% of Americans rate either major party favorably, and individual politicians like Mamdani may poll considerably better than the organizations they are associated with[17]. Democrats pursuing a House majority need 218 seats, and the tension between energizing safe urban districts versus fielding electable moderates in competitive ones remains unresolved[14].

Beyond the primary battlefield, the fight over voting rules is emerging as a defining fault line between the parties — and a potential drag on Republican legislative cohesion. Trump has posted about the SAVE America Act, which would mandate documentary proof of citizenship to register and photo ID to vote, nearly 200 times on Truth Social, and twice threatened to hold other GOP priorities hostage until it passes[16]. That threat became concrete when Trump abruptly cancelled the signing ceremony for the ROAD to Housing Act — a bill that had cleared the House 358-32 and the Senate 85-5 — conditioning his signature on passage of the voter ID legislation[18]. The maneuver blindsided Senate Majority Leader John Thune and Rep. French Hill, the latter of whom was actively touting the bill at a press conference when Trump pulled the plug[18]. The SAVE America Act faces steep arithmetic in the Senate, likely falling short of both the 60 votes needed to break a filibuster and potentially even a simple majority, meaning Trump's leverage gambit may simply kill popular bipartisan legislation without delivering his electoral priority[18]. Both Trump and DNC Chair Jaime Harrison have framed their competing voting-rights proposals in nearly identical terms — each claiming elections are only lost through cheating — underscoring how thoroughly the myth of systemic electoral fraud has become a foundational organizing principle for both parties' bases[16].

At the individual politician level, the 2026 popularity landscape reveals a party system in flux. Barack Obama and Bernie Sanders lead approval rankings while Chuck Schumer ranks among the least popular figures in American politics, a pairing that encapsulates the establishment's credibility deficit with both center-left and progressive voters[17]. In Texas, Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico is attempting a different kind of repositioning, delivering an acceptance speech at the state party convention that leaned heavily into eighth-generation Texas roots and invoked Barbara Jordan to argue the state's current political culture is incongruent with its own historical identity[19]. The rhetorical strategy — rooting progressive Democratic politics in regional and ancestral legitimacy rather than national party brand — reflects a broader search for political language that can move voters in structurally hostile terrain[19]. Whether such messaging can overcome Texas's structural Republican advantage, or whether competitive-district moderates like Conley represent the more reliable path to a House majority, will likely define the party's post-2026 strategic debate regardless of the election outcome[14,19].

themes.theme: Supreme Court, Presidential Power & Rule of Law
themes.briefing:
The Supreme Court's end-of-term decisions are reshaping the constitutional architecture of executive power in consequential and, in some respects, contradictory ways. Most significantly, the Court voted 6-3 to strike down the 91-year-old precedent of Humphrey's Executor v. United States, clearing the way for Trump to fire FTC commissioners and extending that authority over approximately two dozen multi-member independent agencies Congress had deliberately insulated from presidential control.[8] Chief Justice Roberts' majority opinion grounded the ruling in accountability logic — that the president must control subordinates who exercise executive power — but Justice Sotomayor's 49-page dissent, joined by Kagan and Jackson, warned the decision confers on the president 'far greater power than ever before' and distorts the constitutional structure of government.[8] The same day, however, the Court drew a boundary: in a 5-4 ruling, it blocked Trump from firing Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook, with Roberts writing that permitting the removal would 'transform the Federal Reserve's for-cause protection into at-will employment' and undermine the nation's tradition of central banking independence.[7] The juxtaposition of these two rulings suggests the majority is not applying a clean unitary executive theory but rather calibrating presidential removal power against institution-specific economic and structural considerations — a doctrinal framework that will generate years of further litigation over where exactly that line falls.

The executive power struggle is not confined to independent agencies. The Trump administration has simultaneously pressed a maximalist interpretation of Article II to justify firing career civil servants, with White House aide James Sherk — author of the Schedule Policy/Career memo asserting legal authority to remove career employees without cause — explicitly arguing that 'every federal employee should serve at the pleasure of the president.'[12] Administration officials pressured the acting head of the Merit Systems Protection Board to subordinate its independence to Office of Legal Counsel opinions on unitary executive theory, treating the MSPB's own adjudicatory role as contingent on ideological compliance.[12] This pattern suggests that the Court's FTC ruling is not merely an abstract doctrinal shift but is being rapidly operationalized across the federal bureaucracy in ways that could hollow out civil service protections well before additional legal challenges are resolved.

Beyond removal power, the Court's term has produced other high-stakes rulings with significant political valence. In a 5-4 decision, Justice Barrett's majority upheld Mississippi's law allowing mail-in ballots postmarked by Election Day to be counted if received within five days after, concluding that federal election-day statutes govern the deadline for voting, not for ballot receipt.[6] Separately, the Court declined to hear Trump's appeal of the $5 million jury verdict in E. Jean Carroll's sexual abuse and defamation case, leaving that judgment intact while a second Carroll verdict of $83 million is expected to arrive on petition.[9] Meanwhile, critics have raised sharp questions about the Court's fidelity to factual records in politically charged cases: historian Timothy Snyder argues the majority ruling permitting deportation of Haitians from Springfield, Ohio operated in an 'openly counter-factual' manner by disregarding evidence of racial motivation that a lower court had previously found sufficient to halt the removals.[11] With eight decisions still pending — including the birthright citizenship case and cases on transgender athletes — and the Court's security apparatus being more than doubled in response to assassination threats and political violence, the institution is simultaneously exercising expanded power and operating under unprecedented personal threat to its members.[10]

publications: Can We Still Govern? by Don Moynihan

big_picture:
The dominant thread running through today's digest is the accelerating concentration of executive authority and its cascading consequences across domestic and foreign policy. The Supreme Court's dismantling of Humphrey's Executor[8] is not an isolated legal development — it is the constitutional capstone enabling the broader policy agenda on display elsewhere: the gutting of USAID despite evidence of catastrophic mortality consequences[29], the judicially contested deportation of Haitian residents from Springfield that the Court's majority upheld against lower-court findings of racial motivation[28], and the ongoing restructuring of independent oversight mechanisms that once acted as friction against rapid unilateral action. Taken together, these moves reflect a coherent, if contested, theory of governance in which speed and presidential discretion displace institutional deliberation — a theory now embedded in constitutional doctrine.

Abroad, the consequences of that same unilateralism are playing out in real time. The U.S.-Iran memorandum, negotiated and apparently abandoned within a fortnight, illustrates the hazard of high-speed diplomacy without durable institutional backing[1,3]. Professor Pape's materialized predictions — commercial shipping attacks, Strait of Hormuz pressure, Israeli military stiffening — suggest the regional escalation ladder is functioning precisely as deterrence theorists would expect when agreements collapse[1,3]. Meanwhile, the foreign aid cuts accelerating global health crises[29] reduce American soft-power leverage precisely when hard-power commitments in the Gulf are intensifying, a strategic incoherence that no amount of military posture can fully offset. The compounding of these pressures raises the threshold question of whether the United States retains the institutional bandwidth — diplomatic, developmental, and military — to manage simultaneous crises of this magnitude.

Domestically, the political system is registering the stress. The Democratic Party's New York primaries reveal a base mobilizing in a Tea Party mirror image[14,17], driven by exactly the constituencies most directly affected by USAID dismantlement, immigration enforcement, and judicial rollback of independent agencies. Yet the AI-investment paradox adds a crucial economic dimension that cuts across partisan lines: hyperscalers are committing $805 billion in capex while their own equities crater and operating cash flows are consumed at a 93% rate, suggesting that the financial architecture underwriting both the current growth narrative and significant political donor networks is more fragile than headline AI optimism implies. If that investment cycle corrects sharply, the political and fiscal assumptions embedded in the current policy environment — from deregulation payoffs to tax-cut sustainability — will require urgent reassessment at precisely the moment when institutional guardrails have been most significantly weakened.
